leaves.title: Verb be — singular: I and you
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about yourself and one other person using the verb 'be' — the very first building block for introducing yourself in English.

Use 'am' with 'I' and 'are' with 'you':

• Full forms: I am / you are
• Contractions: I'm / you're
• Negative: I'm not / you aren't
• Question: Am I...? / Are you...?
• Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. / Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to introduce yourself, say where you're from, and ask someone else simple questions about themselves.
examples: I am Diego. I'm a student.
You are Sara. You're from Chicago.
Am I in room 5? Yes, you are.
commonMistakes: Do not say 'I is' or 'you is' — use 'am' with I and 'are' with you.
Do not say 'Yes, I am not' as a short answer — say 'No, I'm not.'

leaves.title: Verb be — singular: he, she, and it
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about other people and things — not just yourself — using 'he,' 'she,' and 'it.' This builds directly on what you already know about 'I' and 'you.'

Use 'is' with 'he,' 'she,' and 'it':

• Full forms: he is / she is / it is
• Contractions: he's / she's / it's
• Negative: he isn't / she isn't / it isn't
• Question: Is he...? / Is she...? / Is it...?
• Short answers: Yes, he is. / No, she isn't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe a third person — a friend, a colleague, a place — the same way you already describe yourself.
examples: He is a doctor. He's from Peru.
She is my sister. She's a teacher.
It is a big city. It's in Brazil.
commonMistakes: Do not say 'he are' or 'she are' — use 'is' with he/she/it.
Do not forget the apostrophe in contractions: 'hes' is wrong, 'he's' is correct.

leaves.title: Verb be — plural: we, you, and they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about groups of people — including yourself as part of a group — using 'we,' 'you' (more than one person), and 'they.' Now that you can use 'be' for one person at a time, this extends the same idea to more than one.

Use 'are' with 'we,' 'you' (plural), and 'they':

• Full forms: we are / you are / they are
• Contractions: we're / you're / they're
• Negative: we aren't / you aren't / they aren't
• Question: Are we...? / Are you...? / Are they...?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about your team, your class, or a group of friends as a group, not just one person at a time.
examples: We are colleagues. We're from the same office.
You are students. You're in room 6.
They are tourists. They're from Canada.
commonMistakes: Remember 'you' can be singular or plural, but the verb form is always 'are'.
Do not say 'they is' — always 'they are' or 'they're'.

leaves.title: Wh- and How questions with be
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to ask real questions with 'be' — not just yes/no questions, but questions that ask for information, like a name, a place, or an age. This is what you'll actually use to get to know someone.

Question words (who, what, where, when, how) come before the verb be:

• Where are you from?
• How old are you?
• Who is she?

We can contract 'is' after a question word (Where's he from?) but not after a pronoun at the end of the sentence (How old is he? — NOT How old's he?).

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask someone their name, where they're from, and how old they are — real conversation-starter questions.
examples: Where are you from? I'm from Toronto.
How old is she? She's ten.
What's your name? My name is Marco.
commonMistakes: Do not put the verb before the question word: 'Are where you from?' is wrong.
Do not contract 'is' when the sentence ends in a pronoun: 'Where is he?' NOT 'Where's he?'

leaves.title: Singular and plural nouns, a and an
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about one thing versus more than one thing, and how to choose between 'a' and 'an' — two small words you'll use constantly.

Most nouns add -s for the plural:

• a pencil → two pencils
• a key → three keys

Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u):

• a book, a phone, a wallet
• an umbrella, an ID card, an orange

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say whether you have one thing or several, and choose 'a' or 'an' correctly every time.
examples: I have a pencil and two pens.
She has an umbrella and three keys.
It's a photo, not an album.
commonMistakes: Don't forget the -s on plural nouns: 'two pencil' is wrong, 'two pencils' is correct.
Choose 'a'/'an' by the sound, not the spelling: it's 'an hour' (vowel sound) but 'a university' (consonant sound).

leaves.title: This, that, these, and those
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to point to things and say whether they're close to you or farther away — essential for shopping, showing photos, or describing what's around you.

The choice depends on two things: how many, and how close.

• this (singular, near you) — This is my bag.
• that (singular, farther away) — That is your bag.
• these (plural, near you) — These are my keys.
• those (plural, farther away) — Those are your keys.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to point out one or more things nearby or across the room and ask what they are.
examples: This is my phone. That is your phone.
These are new shoes. Those are old shoes.
What's this? It's a key chain.
commonMistakes: Don't use 'this'/'that' with plural nouns — say 'these keys', not 'this keys'.
'These'/'those' need a plural verb: 'These are nice', not 'These is nice'.

leaves.title: Possessive adjectives and possessive 's
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say who something belongs to — a key skill for talking about your family, friends, and belongings.

Possessive adjectives go before a noun:

• I → my, you → your, he → his, she → her, it → its, we → our, you (plural) → your, they → their

For a person's name, add 's:

• Sara's brother, Tom's sister, my parents' house (plural noun ending in -s: add just an apostrophe)

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about your own family and belongings, and ask who things belong to.
examples: This is my brother. His name is Leo.
That's Maria's daughter.
Is this your phone or her phone?
commonMistakes: 'It's' means 'it is'; the possessive form is 'its' with no apostrophe — 'The dog is in its bed.'
Don't say 'the brother of Sara' as your default — 'Sara's brother' is the natural everyday form.

leaves.title: Adjectives: word order and form
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn where to put an adjective in a sentence and how adjectives behave differently from nouns in English.

An adjective goes before the noun it describes:

• a small car (NOT a car small)
• an expensive watch

Adjectives never take a plural -s, even when the noun is plural:

• good cars (NOT goods cars)
• blue keys (NOT blues keys)

An adjective can also come after the verb 'be':

• The car is fast. It's very expensive.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe things correctly, in the right word order, whether you're describing one thing or several.
examples: It's a beautiful city.
They're good cars.
This bag is cheap, but that one is expensive.
commonMistakes: Don't put the adjective after the noun: 'a car small' is wrong.
Don't add -s to an adjective: 'goods cars' is wrong — say 'good cars'.

leaves.title: Simple present — affirmative and negative: I, you, we, they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about habits, routines, and things that are generally true — like what you usually eat or drink — using the simple present.

With I, you, we, and they, use the base form of the verb:

• I have breakfast at home.
• We eat a lot of fruit.

For the negative, use don't + base form:

• I don't drink coffee.
• They don't eat meat.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say what you usually do and don't do, especially around everyday habits like eating and drinking.
examples: I have coffee every morning.
We don't eat breakfast at work.
They drink a lot of tea.
commonMistakes: Don't add -s to the verb with I/you/we/they: 'I haves' is wrong — say 'I have'.
Use 'don't', not 'not', for the negative: 'I not like fish' is wrong — say 'I don't like fish'.

leaves.title: Simple present — questions: I, you, we, they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to ask yes/no questions and give short answers about habits and routines — building directly on the affirmative and negative forms you already know.

Use Do + subject + base verb:

• Do you live in London?
• Do they have a car?

Short answers use do/don't, not a repeat of the full verb:

• Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
• Yes, they do. / No, they don't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask someone about their daily routines and habits, and answer the same questions naturally.
examples: Do you live near here? Yes, I do.
Do they work for a British company? No, they don't.
Do we have time for coffee? Yes, we do.
commonMistakes: Don't forget 'Do' at the start of the question: 'You live in London?' should be 'Do you live in London?'
Short answers don't repeat the main verb: 'Yes, I live' is wrong — say 'Yes, I do'.
